interview_metadata.name: Edgard Franco
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I grew up in Evansville, Indiana, mostly on the east side in a pretty ordinary middle-class neighborhood. My family was the kind that believed you show up on time, help neighbors when they ask, and do not make a big production out of yourself. My dad worked in maintenance and industrial repair, and my mom worked administrative jobs, so I was around practical problem-solving from an early age. I was a quiet kid, always taking apart radios, saving old cameras from garage sales, and drawing maps or robots in the margins of notebooks. In high school I liked math, art, and science fiction more than sports, although I did play some pickup basketball. I went to college for a STEM bachelor's degree and got comfortable with Python, MATLAB, Arduino, and data visualization. After school I worked in data analysis for a while, but over time I got pulled toward the creative side: interactive installations, UX research, digital painting, and the way data can tell a story visually. I am married now, no kids, and I am currently not in the workforce while I regroup and try to build a path toward UX research or an interactive media freelance studio. The big theme of my life is probably trying to reconcile technical precision with a very spontaneous, artistic way of living.

follow_ups.question: What was your home like when you were growing up?
follow_ups.response: Stable, modest, and practical. We had dinner together most nights, watched Colts games on Sundays, and went to local events like the West Side Nut Club Fall Festival when we could.

follow_ups.question: Who influenced you most as a kid?
follow_ups.response: My dad influenced the hands-on repair side, and my mom pushed me to explain things clearly. A high school physics teacher also made electronics feel less mysterious.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The main crossroads was leaving the safer data analyst track. I had a job where I was doing useful work, mostly dashboards, reports, cleaning data, and writing scripts, but I felt like I was slowly becoming a person who only maintained things. Around the same time I was building little Arduino light pieces at home and showing them at small local art gatherings. People responded to those more than I expected. My wife and I talked a lot about money and timing, and I decided to step away rather than immediately take another conventional analyst position. It was scary because I am not naturally organized, but it also made me admit that I wanted work with a human and visual side, not just spreadsheets.

follow_ups.question: When did that happen?
follow_ups.response: The decision built up over a couple years, but the real break happened in the last year or so.

follow_ups.question: What did you do first after stepping away?
follow_ups.response: I made a rough portfolio, took notes on HCI certificate programs, and started prototyping a small installation using sensors and projected visuals.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was both. The dissatisfaction just happened gradually, but the decision to pause regular employment and aim toward UX and interactive media was conscious.

follow_ups.question: Did you set a deadline for yourself?
follow_ups.response: I tried to, but deadlines are my weak spot. I told myself six months for a portfolio and I am still tinkering with it.

follow_ups.question: Who knew about the decision first?
follow_ups.response: My wife knew first. Then I told a couple close friends from my gaming group.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes, probably. A mentor in UX or a local arts-business incubator would have helped me turn vague ideas into steps.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have mattered most?
follow_ups.response: Accountability and introductions, honestly. Someone saying, here are three people to talk to and a date to show work.

follow_ups.question: Did you look for that kind of support?
follow_ups.response: A little, through local arts events, but I was inconsistent about following up.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I am married. My wife is the person I am closest to, and she is much more steady with calendars and bills than I am. We do not have children, which is intentional for now because we are still sorting out career and money questions. My parents are still important to me, and they live in the Evansville area, so I see them maybe a couple times a month. We are not a dramatic family; we mostly show care through practical things, like helping with repairs, checking in by text, or bringing food over. My wife and I spend evenings cooking, watching movies, or just working on separate projects in the same room. I can be solitary, so marriage has taught me to actually say what is going on instead of disappearing into a project for six hours.

follow_ups.question: What does a normal evening with your wife look like?
follow_ups.response: Usually dinner around 7, maybe mushroom risotto or ramen if I am ambitious, then she reads or watches something while I sketch, code, or mess with electronics.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your parents?
follow_ups.response: Usually every other Sunday or so, plus quick visits if somebody needs help with a computer, a shelf, or a car question.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: I have one younger sister. We are friendly but not constantly in touch; we text memes, family updates, and sometimes meet for coffee.

follow_ups.question: Where does she live?
follow_ups.response: She is also in southern Indiana, close enough for family birthdays and holidays.

follow_ups.question: What do you two talk about?
follow_ups.response: Mostly family logistics, movies, and her teasing me about unfinished projects.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: I have a small group of close friends, not a huge social circle. The main group is my tabletop gaming group, four of us who meet about twice a month when scheduling works. I also know people through Hoosier Runners, though those are more activity friends than deep confidants. There are a couple people in the local art scene I see at gallery openings and photography talks. I like people, but I need a lot of alone time, so most of my friendships are built around a shared activity.

follow_ups.question: Who do you spend the most time with outside family?
follow_ups.response: Probably my friend Marcus from tabletop gaming. We trade sci-fi books and argue about camera lenses.

follow_ups.question: Where do you usually meet friends?
follow_ups.response: At someone’s apartment for gaming, a coffee shop, a local gallery opening, or trails when the running club meets.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: We live in Evansville, in the 47715 area, which is convenient but not especially glamorous. There are strip malls, restaurants, grocery stores, apartments, and subdivisions, so it is very practical day to day. I can get to hardware stores, groceries, and coffee without planning much, which suits me. It is car-oriented, but there are pockets where you can walk. I like that I am still close enough to downtown art events and the riverfront, while also not far from roads that get me out toward hiking areas.

follow_ups.question: What places do you visit most nearby?
follow_ups.response: The grocery store, a hardware store, a coffee shop where I sometimes work on my laptop, and whatever pizza place is open late.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A little. We wave and occasionally talk about packages or weather, but we are not in each other’s houses much.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe. I would not leave expensive camera gear visible in the car, but walking around in the evening does not worry me much.

follow_ups.question: Has anything happened that made you cautious?
follow_ups.response: Mostly car break-in stories from neighbors, nothing violent that I have personally experienced.

follow_ups.question: Does your wife feel the same?
follow_ups.response: She is a little more cautious at night, especially in parking lots, but generally comfortable.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is convenience and familiarity. The downside is that it can feel culturally smaller than what I want sometimes, so I drive to Chicago or other cities when I need a bigger art or architecture fix.

follow_ups.question: What keeps you in Evansville?
follow_ups.response: Family, affordability, and the fact that there is enough of an arts scene if you look for it.

follow_ups.question: What frustrates you most?
follow_ups.response: The car dependence and the feeling that creative tech work is harder to find locally.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: It is just me and my wife. We share the place and split the household rhythm pretty naturally: she is better with scheduling and bill reminders, and I handle a lot of cooking, tech fixes, and small repairs. We do not have children or roommates. Our home has too many project bins, camera parts, and notebooks, but it works for us.

follow_ups.question: Who does most household chores?
follow_ups.response: We split them, but not perfectly. I cook more, she keeps us on top of laundry and paperwork, and we both clean when it gets impossible to ignore.

follow_ups.question: Do you both work from home?
follow_ups.response: She has steadier work routines than I do. I mostly work from home on portfolio projects and prototypes right now.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is permanent. It is just the two of us.

follow_ups.question: No one staying short term right now?
follow_ups.response: No, nobody right now.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, it has been stable.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Occasionally a friend might crash after a late game night, but that is rare.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a few times a year.

follow_ups.question: Any family overnight visits?
follow_ups.response: Not usually, since family lives close enough to go home.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, there is no one away who usually lives here.

follow_ups.question: No students or military members?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: No long hospital stays?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: My week is uneven. On Mondays I try to plan, answer emails, and work on my UX portfolio, though sometimes that becomes reorganizing files instead of real progress. Midweek I usually code, sketch interface ideas, or prototype with Arduino and sensors. I run or hike when the weather is decent, often late morning or near sunset. Fridays or Saturdays might include a gallery opening, a film screening, tabletop gaming, or a last-minute drive with a camera. Sundays are usually slower, with groceries, cooking, and sometimes family.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually wake up?
follow_ups.response: Around 8:00 or 8:30 if I do not have something scheduled, earlier on trail-running days.

follow_ups.question: What part of the day is most productive?
follow_ups.response: Late morning for writing or code, late night for art and tinkering, which is not always ideal.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: Right now I am not in the workforce in the formal sense. I am not clocking into a job or getting regular wages. I spend my work-like hours building a portfolio, learning more UX research methods, experimenting with interactive media, and doing occasional unpaid or informal prototype help for friends. In the past I worked as a data analyst, writing Python and MATLAB scripts, cleaning datasets, building visualizations, and explaining results to nontechnical people. I am trying to turn that background into paid work again, but in a more creative direction.

follow_ups.question: Are you actively applying for jobs?
follow_ups.response: Slowly, yes. I have been looking at UX researcher, data visualization, and interactive media developer roles.

follow_ups.question: Do you earn any freelance income now?
follow_ups.response: Not consistently. A little informal money here and there, but not enough to call it a job.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I handle a lot of cooking and household tech issues. I also keep up with my parents a bit, especially if they need help with a device or something around the house. I try to attend Hoosier Runners meetups, although I am irregular. The gaming group requires some prep because I often run the story, so I write scenarios and maps. I also keep a loose notebook of project ideas, though loose is the key word.

follow_ups.question: How much time does gaming prep take?
follow_ups.response: Maybe two or three hours before a session, usually the night before because I procrastinate.

follow_ups.question: What household responsibility is most yours?
follow_ups.response: Cooking and fixing things: routers, shelves, loose cabinet hinges, that sort of thing.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest change is not having a regular work schedule. At first it felt freeing, but then I realized structure does not magically appear. I have been experimenting with blocking mornings for portfolio work and leaving afternoons for errands or prototyping. I also started running with the club more often to give myself at least one fixed thing each week. My wife and I have had to talk more explicitly about money and house routines because my days are less externally organized.

follow_ups.question: Has the change helped your mood?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, because I feel more aligned with what I want. Sometimes it makes me anxious because progress is harder to measure.

follow_ups.question: What routine stuck best?
follow_ups.response: A weekly Sunday grocery and cooking plan has stuck better than my portfolio schedule.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: We do not have children, so there is no school-year routine or after-school activity schedule in our household.

follow_ups.question: Do children factor into your future plans?
follow_ups.response: Maybe, but not immediately. We would need more stability first.

follow_ups.question: Do you spend time with nieces, nephews, or friends’ kids?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally at family gatherings, but I am not a regular caregiver.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My experiences have been limited and mostly routine. I have been pulled over for speeding once or twice, got a warning once and a ticket another time. I have not had a serious personal conflict with police. I do pay attention to how different people experience policing, though, and I know my own experience as a white guy in Indiana is not universal.

follow_ups.question: When was your last police interaction?
follow_ups.response: A traffic stop a few years ago on the way back from a hike.

follow_ups.question: How did it feel?
follow_ups.response: Annoying and tense, but not frightening in the way I know it can be for other people.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Mostly seeing police at local events and traffic accidents. Nothing especially personal stands out beyond traffic stops.

follow_ups.question: Any positive experiences?
follow_ups.response: At public events they have mostly just been present and directing traffic.

follow_ups.question: Any negative experiences involving friends?
follow_ups.response: A friend had a rough traffic stop he felt was unfair, but I was not there.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have never been arrested, and no immediate family member has been arrested that I know of. I know acquaintances with old DUI or possession stories, but not close family.

follow_ups.question: Has that affected your family life?
follow_ups.response: No, not directly.

follow_ups.question: Do you worry about arrest for anyone close to you?
follow_ups.response: No, not in a day-to-day way.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in presidential elections and usually midterms, but I have missed local primaries. I know local elections matter, but I am not as disciplined about them as I should be. I usually research candidates online, check local coverage, and talk with my wife before voting. I am not someone with yard signs everywhere.

follow_ups.question: Do you vote in person or by mail?
follow_ups.response: Usually in person.

follow_ups.question: What elections have you missed?
follow_ups.response: Mostly municipal primaries or smaller local races when I was distracted or traveling.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I would call myself center-left or progressive-leaning independent. I care about civil rights, health care access, climate, public education, and making cities more livable. At the same time, I grew up around people who value work, modesty, and skepticism toward big promises, so I tend to be pragmatic rather than ideological. I am more comfortable with evidence-based policy than slogans. I generally vote Democratic, but I do not feel like a party loyalist. I distrust performative politics from either side, especially online. Locally, I am interested in practical things like transit, arts funding, trails, and whether people can afford rent and health care.

follow_ups.question: What issue matters most to you right now?
follow_ups.response: Health care access and economic stability, partly because being between jobs makes those feel very real.

follow_ups.question: Do your views cause tension with family?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes. Some relatives are more conservative, so I choose my moments and try not to turn every dinner into a debate.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more aware of how fragile people’s finances are, including ours. When I had steady work, I understood health insurance and benefits as policy issues, but now they feel personal. I have also become more skeptical of tech solutionism. I still love technology, but I do not think every social problem needs an app. I am more interested in local institutions, mutual aid, libraries, clinics, and boring infrastructure that actually helps people.

follow_ups.question: Did any event push that shift?
follow_ups.response: Leaving regular employment and comparing health insurance options definitely pushed it.

follow_ups.question: Has your wife influenced your views?
follow_ups.response: Yes. She is practical and asks how any policy would actually work for a household.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They affected me somewhat to a lot, mostly by making me think harder about things I had been able to treat as abstract. I did not grow up thinking of myself as privileged, because my family was modest, but I have had to recognize that being white shaped how safe and normal certain spaces felt to me. The policing conversation especially made me listen more and talk less. I would not claim I became an activist, but it changed what I read and how I interpret news stories.

follow_ups.question: Did you attend protests?
follow_ups.response: I attended one local gathering, but mostly I listened, donated a small amount, and talked with friends.

follow_ups.question: What did you read or watch?
follow_ups.response: Local reporting, long-form essays, and some books and interviews recommended by friends.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the issues are real and not solved by saying most people are individually decent. Systems can produce unfair outcomes even when individuals think they are being reasonable. I think police accountability, mental health response, housing, schools, and economic opportunity are all connected. I also think white people like me need to tolerate discomfort without centering ourselves. That is easier to say than to practice, especially in mixed political company.

follow_ups.question: What conversations have been hardest?
follow_ups.response: Family conversations where someone hears criticism of policing as criticism of every individual officer.

follow_ups.question: What do you think would help locally?
follow_ups.response: Transparent data, community oversight, and more non-police crisis response options.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think about it as history that is still active, not just something from textbooks. Evansville and the Midwest can act like racism is only a Southern or big-city issue, but that is not true. Housing patterns, schools, policing, and who feels welcome in cultural spaces all show it. I have also thought about how my German and Irish family history gave me a sense of ethnic background without the same barriers many other groups face now. So I try to keep learning without pretending I have some perfect answer.

follow_ups.question: Does this affect your art or work ideas?
follow_ups.response: Yes, it makes me more careful about whose story a data visualization is telling and who gets to interpret it.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about race with friends?
follow_ups.response: With some friends, yes. It depends on the relationship and whether the conversation can be honest.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I have talked with friends and my wife, attended one local event, and donated small amounts when I could. I am more of a listener and reader than a public organizer.

follow_ups.question: Did you post about it online?
follow_ups.response: Very little. I do not like performative posting, so I shared a couple resources and mostly stayed quiet.

follow_ups.question: Have you changed any behavior?
follow_ups.response: I pay more attention to local candidates’ positions on policing and equity.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My wife is thoughtful about it and probably more direct than I am. My close friends are mostly sympathetic, though we vary in how active we are. Some older relatives are skeptical and feel like the conversation unfairly paints police or white working people as villains. I try to avoid caricaturing them, but I also push back when someone says racism is basically over. It is one of those topics where I choose smaller conversations over big arguments.

follow_ups.question: Who do you talk to most about it?
follow_ups.response: My wife and Marcus, because they can disagree without turning it into a fight.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone changed their mind?
follow_ups.response: A little, maybe. More often people soften one claim rather than completely change views.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I am in decent health. I am 33, no major chronic illness that I know of, and I can hike and run when I keep a routine. My weak spots are sleep, stress, and inconsistent exercise. I get some neck and wrist soreness from computer and electronics work. I could eat healthier, but I do cook a lot at home. Mentally, I deal with anxiety more than I used to, especially around career uncertainty.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a primary care doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yes, though I am not great about going unless something is clearly wrong.

follow_ups.question: How often do you exercise?
follow_ups.response: Anywhere from once to four times a week, depending on weather, motivation, and whether I am buried in a project.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: It is easy when I have a scheduled run, a hike planned, or groceries in the house. It is hard when I stay up late working on a prototype and then order pizza the next day because I am tired. I like cooking, so food is not the main barrier; consistency is. Having no fixed work schedule also makes it easy to drift.

follow_ups.question: What healthy meal do you make often?
follow_ups.response: Rice bowls, ramen with vegetables, or mushroom risotto if I have time.

follow_ups.question: What derails you fastest?
follow_ups.response: Late nights and a project that is almost working.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing huge like a broken bone or major diagnosis. I did have a period where my wrist and forearm hurt enough that I worried about repetitive strain, so I changed my desk setup and took breaks more seriously. I also had a stretch of poor sleep and anxiety when I was deciding whether to leave regular work. I got a basic checkup, and nothing dramatic came back. It was more of a warning that I cannot run indefinitely on coffee and late-night focus.

follow_ups.question: Did you get treatment for the wrist pain?
follow_ups.response: Just a doctor visit, stretching, ergonomic changes, and less marathon soldering or coding.

follow_ups.question: Is the anxiety diagnosed?
follow_ups.response: Not formally as a disorder. I have discussed it with a doctor, but I am not in regular therapy.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Health has not prevented me from working in a formal sense. Anxiety and sleep problems do affect productivity, especially because I am self-directed right now.

follow_ups.question: Do physical issues limit hiking or running?
follow_ups.response: Only minor things like sore knees or ankles after a long trail.

follow_ups.question: Do you miss responsibilities because of health?
follow_ups.response: Not usually, but I can lose a morning after a bad sleep night.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: A little. My parents are aging, and while they are mostly okay, there are more doctor appointments and minor scares than there used to be. My dad has the usual wear and tear from physical work, and my mom keeps an eye on blood pressure. Nothing has taken over my life, but I can feel the shift where I may need to be more available. My wife and I also talk about how family health could affect our plans.

follow_ups.question: Do you help with appointments?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally I drive or help them understand online portals and forms.

follow_ups.question: Does that worry you financially?
follow_ups.response: Some, because elder care can get expensive fast.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: We have generally gotten care when needed, but cost and insurance are stressful. Since I am not working, benefits are a bigger household conversation. I have delayed things like dental work or a non-urgent appointment because I wanted to see what it would cost. I would not say we have gone without emergency care, but we do weigh whether something is worth the bill. That is a very American sentence, unfortunately.

follow_ups.question: What care have you delayed?
follow_ups.response: Dental cleaning once, eye exam stuff, and getting the wrist looked at sooner.

follow_ups.question: Who handles insurance paperwork?
follow_ups.response: My wife is better at it, but we both look at bills because they are confusing.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Nothing major or formal. We use ordinary home remedies: tea, stretching, heat packs, maybe a massage tool for sore muscles. I have tried mindfulness apps and breathing exercises when anxious. I respect some non-Western practices, but I am pretty evidence-minded and would not use alternatives instead of needed medical care.

follow_ups.question: Any supplements?
follow_ups.response: Vitamin D sometimes in winter, but not a big supplement routine.

follow_ups.question: Any chiropractic or acupuncture?
follow_ups.response: No regular use. I have considered acupuncture for tension but have not done it.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not smoke. I drink socially, mostly beer at a game night or a gallery opening, but I am not a heavy drinker. During tough times I am more likely to stay up too late, disappear into a project, or eat badly than drink a lot. I have noticed that alcohol makes anxiety and sleep worse, so I keep it moderate.

follow_ups.question: How often do you drink?
follow_ups.response: Maybe once a week or less, usually one or two drinks.

follow_ups.question: What do you do instead when stressed?
follow_ups.response: Walk, cook, play guitar quietly, or tinker with something small.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not rely on prescriptions or pain medication for coping. I take over-the-counter ibuprofen occasionally after a long hike or if my wrist acts up. Marijuana is not a regular thing for me; I have tried it socially in the past, but it is not part of my routine and sometimes makes me feel more anxious. My most recent substance use was probably a beer with friends and ibuprofen after a trail run.

follow_ups.question: Any prescribed mental health medication?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Any concern about substance use in the household?
follow_ups.response: No, not really.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: Carefully. We budget for premiums, copays, and prescriptions, and we try not to ignore preventive care even when it is annoying. My wife’s steadier income helps. We keep some savings, but a large medical bill would be stressful. I also try to stay healthy in boring ways, like cooking at home and getting outside, because prevention feels cheaper than crisis.

follow_ups.question: Do you have emergency savings?
follow_ups.response: Some, but not as much as I would like.

follow_ups.question: What bill worries you most?
follow_ups.response: A surprise emergency room bill or dental work.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally pro-vaccine. I got COVID shots and boosters when recommended, and I get flu shots most years.

follow_ups.question: Were you hesitant at all?
follow_ups.response: Not much. I read about side effects, but I trusted the overall evidence.

I hope my wife and I have more financial breathing room, maybe a house with a garage or spare room for a real workshop. I want to keep hiking, cooking, playing guitar, and running tabletop games, because those things make me feel like myself. I also want to be less avoidant about deadlines and more reliable without becoming rigid. And yes, I still want to photograph Kyoto someday.

follow_ups.question: What is the first step toward that future?
follow_ups.response: Finish the portfolio and apply consistently instead of endlessly polishing.

follow_ups.question: Would you stay in Evansville?
follow_ups.response: Possibly, especially if remote work makes it viable. I like having roots here.

transcript.question_text: What do you value the most in your life?
transcript.response: I value curiosity, loyalty, and making things that help people see differently. My marriage matters most day to day, because it is where my abstract values get tested in practical ways. I value enough independence to think and create, but also enough community that I do not disappear into myself. I care about craft, honesty, and modest usefulness. I would rather make a small thing that genuinely connects with people than chase status.

follow_ups.question: What value did you learn from your parents?
follow_ups.response: Reliability and not acting like you are above practical work.

follow_ups.question: What value feels most your own?
follow_ups.response: Curiosity, especially crossing technical and artistic boundaries.
